The excrements of the first and second <term>coction</term> <gloss>digestion or "cooking" of nutrients</gloss> (namely in the intestines, and the vesicles of urine and gall) are coexistent with the digesting organs themselves. Finally, not only in the vegetative part of the soul, but even before the soul itself, there is a mind, providence, and intellect; these dispose, order, and provide all things immediately from the first origin toward the being and well-being of the chick; and by art they fashion it into the form and likeness of the parents.

Regarding this likeness of the offspring, one may wonder what the cause is that sometimes the <term>foetus</term> <gloss>offspring/fetus</gloss> is found more similar to the father, sometimes to the mother, and sometimes even to ancestors, whether paternal or maternal? Especially since in one mating, and at the same moment, several eggs are fecundated. It is also wonderful that virtues and vices, diseases as well, and even scars and birthmarks, are transferred from parents to their descendants; and this only to certain offspring, but not to all. In the race of poultry, some are noble and born for battle, who prefer to die rather than yield to adversaries by fleeing; yet their grandsons, unless they were born from similar parents, gradually cast off that virtue, according to the saying: the brave are created by the brave. In most other species of animals also (and especially in humans) a nobility of race is observed; and many gifts of mind and body come to them by descent.

I have often wondered at this: why, since we see the offspring (for the most part) obtain a certain mixed structure or composition from both parents, and this in all other parts; yet the same does not happen in the genitals: but for the most part either a male or a female is born, and very rarely indeed a <term>hermaphroditus</term> <gloss>hermaphrodite</gloss>?

Finally, many things are present before they appear; and some are begun among the first things which are finished last, such as the eyes, the genitals, and the beak.

Certain doubts and difficulties also arise from this concerning the primacy of the limbs or the dignity of the parts;

<summary>Harvey explores the hereditary transmission of physical and behavioral traits from parents to offspring and questions why sexual organs remain distinct rather than mixed. He notes that vital structures are often initiated long before they are fully formed.</summary>
